ageing_relevance.rationale: About a quarter of CST3 papers mention ageing, and it is linked to age-related macular degeneration, chronic kidney disease and cardiovascular disease. The strongest links are to rare amyloidoses. The project context describes a methylation surrogate, not the measured protein.

evidence.value: One of seven plasma proteins whose DNA-methylation surrogates make up the GrimAge clock.

background_knowledge: Cystatin C is widely used as a kidney-function biomarker, which probably inflates the ageing-related literature count.

mechanism.rationale: CST3 is a secreted cysteine protease inhibitor. Whether raising or lowering it would slow ageing is unclear, because it works as a biomarker and has context-dependent roles.

evidence.value: As an inhibitor of cysteine proteinases, this protein is thought to serve an important physiological role as a local regulator of this enzyme activity

background_knowledge: Higher plasma cystatin C tracks reduced kidney function and cardiovascular risk. In Alzheimer disease models it has been reported as neuroprotective. Variants form amyloid in hereditary cerebral haemorrhage.

tractability.rationale: There is small-molecule evidence (a structure with ligand and a high-quality pocket) and antibody feasibility because the protein is secreted. PROTAC and other modalities have little support, and no approved-drug precedent is listed.

safety.rationale: Open Targets lists no liabilities, but the absence of data is not evidence of safety. Inhibiting a protease inhibitor could raise protease activity, and CST3 variants cause amyloid disease.
background_knowledge: Loss of an endogenous protease inhibitor could cause unwanted protease activity. This inference is not backed by the tool data.

clinical_precedence.rationale: No drugs acting on CST3 are listed in the clinic.

assessment.summary: CST3 (cystatin C) is a secreted cysteine protease inhibitor and a GrimAge component. About 25% of its papers concern ageing, and it is associated with age-related macular degeneration, chronic kidney disease and aging. Its strongest disease links are to rare amyloidoses. The tools show moderate tractability (a small-molecule pocket and antibody feasibility), no listed safety liabilities and no clinical drugs. The direction of modulation is unclear, and the project evidence concerns only the methylation surrogate, not the measured protein. Recommendation: deprioritise as a drug target, though it remains useful as a biomarker.
key_uncertainties: Whether raising or lowering CST3 activity slows ageing: causal evidence such as Mendelian randomisation independent of kidney function would resolve this.
Whether the ageing literature and associations reflect biomarker or kidney-function confounding rather than a causal role.
The CST3 surrogate was not tested in schizophrenia in Part 1, and surrogate levels may not reflect measured protein.
Safety is untested: there is no data on the effects of chronic modulation.
source_conflicts: Tractability lists small-molecule and antibody evidence, but the clinical candidates list shows no drugs. I relied on the clinical list for precedence and scored tractability as moderate.
Literature gives a 24.6% ageing share, but the top disease associations are rare amyloidoses, and the ageing-related associations score only 0.1-0.47. I treated ageing relevance as moderate.
